pr_title: Use operations in our analyzers that need symbols
pr_body:
Fixes: #16922

This change updates our analyzers that need access to the symbols to use
`IOperation` where possible. Using syntax analysis for this kind of
analyzer has worse performance. These analyzers run on generated code,
which can include EF migrations, the design of which amplifies these
effects.

On the path to this, I also added support for a few more cases that
operations make easy. Since we're doing this anyway, I want to have
confidence that we're checking everything (within reason). In some cases
the diagnostic experience changed a bit (including more of the
declaration/code) - I felt like all of these were OK changes. Given the
kinds of error message reported by the analyzers "don't use that type"
it seems like it's still a good enough experience without
micro-optimizing all of the locations.
pr_comments:
> We want to report diagnostics on usage of symbols defined in our library (operations)

Ah got it, sorry your implementation is correct then.
@pranavkm - SUPER ready for you to review.

issue_context.title: Analyzer processing of generated code causes significant slowdown in build
issue_context.body:
After investigating the slow build times of an EF Core sample project (https://github.com/aspnet/EntityFrameworkCore/issues/18618), it turned out the slowdown is coming from the ASP.NET analyzers. EF Core migrations are generated code which particularly affect analysis time - as a general rule it seems that analyzers should opt out of generated code analysis (via [ConfigureGeneratedCodeAnalysis](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.diagnostics.analysiscontext.configuregeneratedcodeanalysis?view=roslyn-dotnet#Microsoft_CodeAnalysis_Diagnostics_AnalysisContext_ConfigureGeneratedCodeAnalysis_Microsoft_CodeAnalysis_Diagnostics_GeneratedCodeAnalysisFlags_)) unless they have a good reason.

To repro, clone https://github.com/roji/AnalyzerBuildPerf. On my machine, building this project with `Microsoft.NET.Sdk` takes about 6s, while building it with `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web` takes about 16s. While this repro project is somewhat heavy, it does seem realistic, and various other generated code scenarios may be even much, much worse.

Analyzer packages being brought in by `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web` are Microsoft.AspNetCore.Analyzers, Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Analyzers and Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Analyzers.

Area | Analyzer  | Status
-- | -- | --
Analyzers (top-level) | All |  Opts out of generated code analysis
MVC | AttributesShouldNotBeAppliedToPageModelAnalyzer | Opts out of generated code analysis
MVC | AvoidHtmlPartialAnalyzer (extends ViewFeatureAnalyzerBase) | **Does not contain any setting**
MVC | TagHelpersInCodeBlocksAnalyzer | *Explicitly opts into generated code analysis*
MVC | TopLevelParameterNameAnalyzer | Opts out of generated code analysis
Components | ComponentParameterAnalyzer | **Does not contain any setting**
Components | ComponentParameterUsageAnalyzer | *Explicitly opts into generated code analysis*
Components | ComponentInternalUsageDiagnosticAnalyzer (uses InternalUsageAnalyzer) | **Does not contain any setting**

Note that generated code analysis is on by default. Seems like a pass should be done and at least some (if not all?) of these should opt out (although am not aware of the status of code-generated Razor code and what you want to analyze there).
comments: Thanks for the analysis @roji.  I know for some of these, the need to analyze the C# parts of razor code means they *do* need to analyze generated code, but you're right that at least the ones with no setting should be reviewed.

All of the bolded ones **specifically** target Razor. 

There's a way to get a [breakdown of individual analyzer times as well](https://m0sa.net/posts/2019-08-roslyn-analyzer-runtime-performance/). I'm sure we can figure out a way to optimize this more.

How it be and what it do:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1430011/68493514-7175f480-0201-11ea-9bfa-472285035e28.png)

Ideally Roslyn would support a finer-grained "tag" that would allow analyzers to process Razor files but not EF migrations, or vice versa. Just a blanket "is it code-generated" seems like it may not be enough.

Cool, @rynowak I wish I knew about that analyzer breakdown option when I started looking at this :)

Note the recommendation in https://github.com/aspnet/EntityFrameworkCore/issues/18618#issuecomment-547043966, to move away from SyntaxNode/GetSymbolInfo to an IOperation-based analyzer. Could help if you really need those analyzers to run.

Yup. Agreed.

Profiles confirm that what's expensive here is doing syntax-driven analysis but then asking for symbols. Both of these were written pre-operations I think - the component one is a clone of the EF internal usage analyzer but with generated code analysis on. Compare with the perf results for [this](https://github.com/aspnet/AspNetCore/blob/master/src/Components/Analyzers/src/ComponentParameterUsageAnalyzer.cs) which runs on generated code and uses operations to do a pretty similar task to `ComponentInternalUsageDiagnosticAnalyzer`,

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1430011/68494569-818ed380-0203-11ea-8405-08b2dc6fbcf8.png)

Oh, nice. We already have https://github.com/aspnet/EntityFrameworkCore/issues/18637 tracking rewriting our own analyzer with operations, but it's much less urgent since it simply skips generated code. If you do it on your side I'll be happy to copy-paste though :)
FYI opened https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/issues/39758 for Roslyn support selective generated code analysis.

Here's an update with the results of https://github.com/aspnet/AspNetCore/pull/17001

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1430011/68725827-737ae300-0574-11ea-9dda-f9b573ac9a79.png)

I'm still not super thrilled with that, and digging deeper.

@mavasani - any advice on a non-allocating way to get the containing namespace of a symbol and compare to a known value?

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1430011/68726963-edf93200-0577-11ea-96e9-07dfbc9b184b.png)

https://github.com/aspnet/AspNetCore/blob/master/src/Components/Analyzers/src/ComponentInternalUsageDiagnosticAnalzyer.cs#L35

I guess I could start with `.RenderTree` and then walk up through `.ContainingNamespace`
You shouldn't compare symbols by their fully qualified names or display strings. Your approach of comparing each namespace name and walking up the containing namespace chain seems correct.

@rynowak it might be good to also implement [@mavasani's suggestion](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/issues/39758#issuecomment-553155652) to programmatically ignore generated code unless it's Razor (the question would be how to identify them - extension?). This would cut out all the EF migrations.

review_comments:
I think you can probably do couple of tweaks here:

1. Extract out the logic into a common helper `void VisitSymbol(ISymbol symbol, Action<Diagnostic> reportDiagnostic, Location location, SymbolDisplayFormat format)`
2. Maintain a per-compilation cache of processed symbols so you avoid duplicate processing of symbols and also duplicate diagnostics for the same symbol.

> Maintain a per-compilation cache of processed symbols so you avoid duplicate processing of symbols and also duplicate diagnostics for the same symbol.

How would this help?
- We want to report diagnostics on *usage* of symbols defined in our library (operations)
- We want to report diagnostics on *declarations* based on symbols defined in our library (symbols)

My assumption is that our symbol action is going to be called once-per-declaration in user code - preventing duplicates in reporting errors for those sites.

This appears to be a behavior difference between operations and symbols. When I get the symbol through an `IOperation` the receiver is the class (static extension method), the existing code expect the receiver to be the `this IHtmlHelper helper` parameter.

/cc @mavasani in case he has any idea
Either way I don't think checking this is critical for our success.
